useCases.title: Selective session removal
useCases.scenario: An application displays several signed-in contexts and must remove only the selected one.

useCases.title: Controlled post-sign-out navigation
useCases.scenario: A product requires users to land on a specific page after authentication ends.

interview.question: What does signOut() do in a multi-session application?
interview.answer: In a multi-session application, signOut() without options signs out all users on the current client. A sessionId option narrows the action to one session.
interview.followUp: How can the post-sign-out destination be controlled? Pass redirectUrl in the sign-out options.

interview.question: How would you wire a custom React sign-out button?
interview.answer: Use the signOut method exposed by useClerk() in a React custom flow. Invoke it from the event handler for the sign-out control.
interview.followUp: What alternative access pattern does the documentation describe? The Clerk object can also provide the signOut() method.

interview.question: Which options can be passed to signOut()?
interview.answer: The method accepts an optional options object. Its documented options include redirectUrl for navigation after completion and sessionId for selecting a particular session.
interview.followUp: When is sessionId especially useful? It is useful when a multi-session application needs to remove only one session rather than all active sessions.

keyPoints: A custom React flow gets the sign-out operation from the useClerk() hook.
Calling signOut() without a session identifier ends every active session on the current client.
The no-argument form is the appropriate choice for an everywhere-style sign-out action.

Setup & components::Appearance customiza.summary: Customize Clerk's prebuilt components with the appearance prop. Apply shared styling at the Clerk integration boundary or target one component with theme, variables, and elements settings.
Setup & components::Appearance customiza.explanation: Clerk's appearance configuration lets you adapt prebuilt components to an application's visual system. Put shared settings on the provider for broad coverage, or place appearance on an individual component for local changes; use theme, variables, and elements for progressively finer control.

parameters.name: appearance
parameters.description: Appearance configuration containing shared or component-specific visual customization, including theme, variables, and elements settings.

parameters.name: appearance.elements
parameters.description: Mapping of Clerk component element names to custom style classes or values.

Setup & components::Appearance customiza.returns: A configured Clerk component tree rendered with the requested appearance customization.

example.title: Customize a Clerk component element
example.explanation: Applies a custom class to a Clerk component element through the provider-level appearance configuration.

useCases.title: Apply shared application styling
useCases.scenario: Several Clerk components should share the product's visual language.

useCases.title: Customize an individual component
useCases.scenario: One prebuilt component needs a targeted visual adjustment.

useCases.title: Style component elements
useCases.scenario: A button, avatar, or other internal part needs a specific class or state style.

interview.question: How can Clerk components be restyled consistently across an application?
interview.answer: Use the `appearance` prop. It can be configured globally where the Clerk integration is initialized, commonly on `ClerkProvider`, or supplied to an individual Clerk component.
interview.followUp: How would you style a component opened by another component? Pass an appearance configuration through the dedicated props object of the component that opens it, because top-level appearance only affects its direct recipient.

interview.question: What does the `elements` property customize?
interview.answer: Use `appearance.elements` to add custom styles to the underlying DOM elements of Clerk's prebuilt components. This provides targeted element-level customization rather than only broad theme settings.
interview.followUp: What is the scope of a provider-level appearance object? It supplies shared styling to components under that integration, while an appearance object placed on a component is local to that component.

interview.question: What limitation applies when one Clerk component opens another?
interview.answer: The top-level appearance prop affects only the component receiving it. A nested or opened component requires appearance to be supplied through that component's dedicated props object.
interview.followUp: Why is this distinction useful? It prevents assuming that styling a trigger automatically propagates to a separately rendered dialog or panel.

keyPoints: Choose provider-level configuration for shared styling or attach the prop directly when only one Clerk component needs customization.
Global appearance belongs at the SDK integration boundary; the exact location depends on the Clerk SDK.
In common Clerk integrations, configure shared appearance on ClerkProvider.
Theme settings provide a focused way to override visual defaults without individually styling every element.
Use state-aware or element-specific customization when broad theme changes are insufficient.
Use elements for direct styling of named parts inside prebuilt Clerk components.
gotchas: Provider or component-level appearance does not automatically style a component opened by another component; pass appearance through that component's dedicated props object.
Element customization targets Clerk's underlying component elements, so choose the documented element key rather than assuming a wrapper or arbitrary selector.

Setup & components::Environment keys.summary: Separate Clerk's publishable and secret keys: expose the publishable key to frontend code and keep the secret key server-side. Use development or production keys according to the Clerk instance.
Setup & components::Environment keys.explanation: Clerk uses one environment key for browser-side initialization and another for backend access. The publishable key identifies the Clerk instance and may be exposed through the framework's public-variable convention, while the secret key authorizes backend access and must remain server-side.

example.title: Separate Clerk environment keys
example.code:
# .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_...
CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_...
example.explanation: Put the publishable key in the client-visible environment variable and keep the secret key in a server-only variable.

useCases.title: Frontend initialization
useCases.scenario: A browser application needs to initialize Clerk.

useCases.title: Backend integration
useCases.scenario: Server code calls Clerk's backend services.

useCases.title: Environment-specific configuration
useCases.scenario: The same application is deployed locally and to production.

interview.question: Which Clerk keys belong in frontend and backend code?
interview.answer: Use a publishable key in the frontend and a secret key in the backend. The publishable key uses a framework-appropriate public environment-variable name, while CLERK_SECRET_KEY must stay server-side.
interview.followUp: Why can the publishable key be client-visible? It identifies the Clerk app for frontend access, whereas the secret key is the credential used for backend access.

interview.question: How do you distinguish development and production keys?
interview.answer: Development keys begin with pk_test_ and sk_test_, while production keys begin with pk_live_ and sk_live_. Configure the appropriate pair through environment variables for each deployment environment.
interview.followUp: What deployment failure can result from using the wrong pair? The app may connect to the wrong Clerk instance or environment, so production should explicitly use the live keys.

interview.question: How should environment-variable names differ between client and server?
interview.answer: The frontend receives the publishable key during Clerk initialization, commonly through a public framework prefix such as NEXT_PUBLIC_. The backend reads CLERK_SECRET_KEY from a server-side environment variable for access to Clerk's backend services.
interview.followUp: How should a Vite application name the client variable? Use VITE_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, while keeping CLERK_SECRET_KEY unprefixed so it is not bundled for the browser.

keyPoints: Configure a publishable key for the frontend so Clerk can initialize in the browser.
Configure the secret key for backend code that communicates with Clerk.
The two keys connect the application to its Clerk instance.
Development publishable keys start with pk_test_, while production publishable keys start with pk_live_.
Development secret keys start with sk_test_, while production secret keys start with sk_live_.
Read CLERK_SECRET_KEY from a server-side environment variable rather than embedding it in application code.
gotchas: Never place CLERK_SECRET_KEY in a public or client-exposed environment variable; doing so exposes the backend credential.

Setup & components::Local development.summary: Use a Clerk Development instance for local authentication and testing. It has separate users, a relaxed security posture, and a 100-user cap, so it must not be used for production.
Setup & components::Local development.explanation: For local work, Clerk uses a Development instance rather than a production workload. This instance has a more relaxed security posture, supports local authentication, and keeps its users separate from other instances. Because the local frontend and Clerk's development API use different domains, Clerk uses development-specific session handling internally.

example.title: Use a development instance locally
example.explanation: Configure the app with the development publishable key, then run it locally and create test users in the development instance.

useCases.title: Local application development
useCases.scenario: Build and test authentication locally with users isolated from production.

useCases.title: Pre-production testing
useCases.scenario: Try Clerk configuration and sign-in flows before release.

useCases.title: Session integration testing
useCases.scenario: Validate cross-site session behavior between localhost and Clerk's development API.

interview.question: What is a Clerk Development instance used for?
interview.answer: A Development instance is Clerk's default instance type for local development. It supports local authentication but has a relaxed security posture, so it is not appropriate for production.
interview.followUp: What happens if the app is deployed with development configuration? The development-specific setup can break in production, so production configuration and a production instance are required.

interview.question: What limitations apply to users in a Development instance?
interview.answer: Development instances isolate local users and settings from other instances. They are also limited to 100 users, and user data cannot be transferred directly between instances.
interview.followUp: How should users be moved to production? Clerk's documented migration path must be used; users cannot simply be migrated from a Development instance to a Production instance.

interview.question: Why does Clerk handle sessions differently during local development?
interview.answer: Local frontends commonly run on localhost while the development FAPI runs on an accounts.dev domain. Since that is cross-site, Clerk uses a development-specific dev-browser mechanism and transmits its state through __clerk_db_jwt instead of relying on cookies.
interview.followUp: Should application code read __clerk_db_jwt? No. It is an internal development mechanism and relying on it causes production failures.

keyPoints: Clerk creates Development as the default instance type for getting started locally.
Its configuration is designed to make local authentication and development easier.
A Development instance supports no more than 100 users.
Users and their data do not transfer directly between Clerk instances.
Cross-site local development prevents dependable cookie-based client-token storage.
Clerk transmits development session state through a query-string value instead of a cookie.
gotchas: Do not use the development instance for production workloads.
The development instance has a 100-user limit.

Setup & components::Provider setup.sourceTitle: <ClerkProvider> component - UI components - React | Clerk Docs
Setup & components::Provider setup.summary: Wrap the React application with ClerkProvider so descendant Clerk hooks and components can access authentication context. Place it at the entry point for app-wide access, or deeper when only part of the tree needs Clerk.
Setup & components::Provider setup.explanation: Place ClerkProvider at the application entry point and pass the publishable key when the SDK requires it. Components and hooks below the provider can then consume Clerk's session and user context; a narrower provider placement is also possible when authentication is needed only in part of the tree.

parameters.name: publishableKey
parameters.description: The application's publishable key, typically read from a client-safe environment variable.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: Optional initial state of the Clerk client during server-side rendering.

Setup & components::Provider setup.returns: A provider component that supplies Clerk session and user context to its descendant hooks and components.

example.title: Wrap a React app with ClerkProvider
example.code:
import React from 'react'
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client'
import App from './App'
import { ClerkProvider } from '@clerk/react'

const publishableKey = import.meta.env.VITE_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY
if (!publishableKey) throw new Error('Missing Clerk Publishable Key')

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <ClerkProvider publishableKey={publishableKey}>
      <App />
    </ClerkProvider>
  </React.StrictMode>,
)
example.explanation: The provider surrounds the application and receives the public key, allowing descendant Clerk components and hooks to access authentication context.

useCases.title: Provide global auth context
useCases.scenario: The whole application uses Clerk authentication and user-aware UI.

useCases.title: Scope authentication to a subtree
useCases.scenario: Only selected routes or components require Clerk functionality.

useCases.title: Configure the publishable key
useCases.scenario: A React app needs to initialize Clerk from browser configuration.

interview.question: What does ClerkProvider provide?
interview.answer: ClerkProvider is required to integrate Clerk into a React application. It supplies session and user context to Clerk hooks and components below it.
interview.followUp: Where should it usually be mounted? At the entry point around the application, unless only a smaller subtree needs authentication.

interview.question: Where should ClerkProvider be placed?
interview.answer: The recommended placement is at the app entry point so authentication is globally accessible. It can instead be rendered deeper in the component tree for a limited part of the application.
interview.followUp: What security rule applies to the key? Use the publishable key in client setup and never expose the secret key in client code.

interview.question: How is ClerkProvider configured in a basic app?
interview.answer: A React app commonly imports ClerkProvider from @clerk/react, reads the publishable key from an environment variable, and renders the app as its child. The provider then makes Clerk context available to descendants.
interview.followUp: What additional provider property may be used in server-rendered applications? An initial Clerk client state can be supplied for SSR, although normal apps do not need to set it.

keyPoints: Add ClerkProvider to a React application before using Clerk's hooks and components.
Descendant Clerk hooks and UI components receive session and user context through the provider.
Mount the provider around the complete application entry point for app-wide authentication access.
An application-wide wrapper lets authentication be consumed throughout the component tree.
A nested provider is appropriate when only selected routes or application sections need Clerk.
Restricting the provider's scope can limit Clerk functionality to the area that needs it.
gotchas: Do not manually provide the initial client state for ordinary application development.
